title: Lesson 18: System Limits: Governor, API, and Storage Limits, and Planning Around Them
description: Governors exist to keep a multitenant platform fair. Learn the limits, then bulkify, batch, and monitor so they never fire on your watch.

questions.question: A single transaction calls update once on a list of 12,000 records. Why does it fail?
options: The 150-statement DML limit is exceeded by the bulk call
The 10,000-row DML limit is exceeded even though one statement was issued
The 50,000-row SOQL retrieval limit is exceeded by the query
The cumulative callout timeout is exceeded by the callouts that were made
questions.explanation: Statement count and row count are separate governors: one update call is a single statement but processes 12,000 rows, past the 10,000-row ceiling.

questions.question: An org's daily API allocation is best understood as which combination?
options: A flat amount that is determined only by the org's edition
A per-user count that ignores platform license types
A fixed cap that cannot be raised by buying any more capacity
A base amount plus a per-license amount plus any add-ons
questions.explanation: The daily request budget is a base figure, plus an amount contributed by the licenses held, plus any add-ons purchased, which is why license mix drives capacity.

questions.question: Why does moving a large volume into Batch Apex succeed where one synchronous transaction failed?
options: Batch Apex raises the per-transaction DML row ceiling
Batch Apex compresses the records so that fewer rows are processed
Batch Apex disables governor limits for asynchronous code
Each chunk runs as its own transaction with a fresh set of limits
questions.explanation: The constraint was the shape of the work, not the total volume: splitting it into chunks gives each chunk its own transaction and its own fresh limits.
